title: Indirect Prompt Injection - Production Attack Surface

questions.question: What distinguishes indirect prompt injection (IPI) from direct prompt injection?
options: IPI requires fine-tuning the target model
IPI embeds instructions inside external content (web pages, emails, tool outputs) that the agent consumes during normal operation, without the attacker touching the user's prompt
IPI is a synonym for jailbreaking
IPI only works on multimodal models
questions.explanation: The lesson defines IPI as embedding instructions inside external content (a web page, email, or tool output) that the agent consumes during normal operation, so the attacker never touches the user's prompt directly -- unlike direct injection.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three IPI delivery vectors listed in the lesson?
options: Direct system-prompt edits by the user
questions.explanation: The lesson's three delivery vectors are RAG (poisoned retrieval), inbox/document workflows, and tool output; a user directly editing the system prompt is not IPI at all since IPI specifically bypasses the user-facing input.

questions.question: Why do user-input filters miss IPI?
options: The payload never appears in the user's input; it appears in retrieved or tool-supplied content
Filters only run after the model responds
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that a filter gated on user input never sees the IPI payload, since it lives in the retrieved document or tool output that gets concatenated into the prompt after the user's turn.

questions.question: What is the central principle of Information Flow Control (IFC) for AI agents?
options: Label content by source as trusted or untrusted; actions triggered by untrusted content must be ratified by trusted input before execution
questions.explanation: The lesson describes IFC as labeling the user's query trusted and retrieved content untrusted, then requiring that any action triggered by untrusted content be ratified by trusted input before it executes -- borrowed from classical OS security.

questions.question: What did Nasr et al. (October 2025, 'The Attacker Moves Second') find about 12 published IPI defenses with adaptive attacks?
options: Adaptive attacks were too expensive to evaluate
Their reported near-zero ASR held under adaptive attack
Adaptive attacks (gradient, RL, random search, human red-team) broke >90% of them despite their original near-zero ASR claims
questions.explanation: The lesson cites Nasr et al.'s finding that adaptive attacks -- gradient search, RL policies, random search, and a 72-hour human red-team -- broke every one of 12 published defenses to over 90% attack success rate, despite their originally reported near-zero ASR.

questions.question: Where does prompt injection rank in the 2025 OWASP LLM Top 10?
questions.explanation: The lesson states OWASP's 2025 LLM Top 10 ranks prompt injection (direct and indirect) as LLM01, the number-one application-layer threat.
